title: THE WOMAN EVERYONE JUDGED WAS THE ONE WHO UNDERSTOOD JESUS—AND THE RELIGIOUS MAN NEVER SAW IT COMING
paragraphs: THE WOMAN EVERYONE JUDGED WAS THE ONE WHO UNDERSTOOD JESUS—AND THE RELIGIOUS MAN NEVER SAW IT COMING

She walked into a room where everyone knew her shame. She left with something no amount of money could buy. And the story Jesus told that night exposes a terrifying possibility: You can sit close to Christ, know the language of religion, and still fail to understand the mercy standing right in front of you.
There is a kind of pain that doesn't come from what people have done to you.
It comes from what they know about you.

The mistakes you cannot undo. The reputation that follows you into rooms. The whispers that suddenly stop when you walk past. The version of your story that people keep repeating long after you've started begging God to change your life.
Imagine carrying all of that into a room full of people who believe they already know exactly who you are.
Now imagine walking straight toward Jesus.
Not because you have an explanation.
Not because you've finally become respectable.
But because somewhere beneath the shame, the regret, and the exhaustion of trying to survive your own past, you have begun to believe that this Man might be different.
That is where one of the most extraordinary encounters in Luke's Gospel begins.
And before this story ends, Jesus will ask a question that reaches far beyond a Pharisee's dining room.
A question that may expose something about our own hearts.
What if the person you consider the greatest sinner understands the grace of God more deeply than you do?
Luke 7:36 tells us that a Pharisee invited Jesus to eat with him.
His name was Simon.
He had a house, a table, and enough social standing to host a respected teacher. Jesus accepted his invitation and reclined at the table, as people commonly did during meals in that culture.
Everything might have appeared respectable.
Until she arrived.
Luke does not give us her name.
It does not tell us her age, her family background, or the precise nature of her sins.
It simply describes her as a woman in the city who was known as a sinner.
The Greek wording is striking:
ἥτις ἦν ἐν τῇ πόλει ἁμαρτωλός
hētis ēn en tē polei hamartōlos
The phrase identifies her as a woman who was known in that city as sinful.
But notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not identify her as a prostitute. It does not tell us that she was Mary Magdalene. It does not give us permission to invent the details of her past.
Whatever her sins were, her reputation was public.
And somehow she learned that Jesus was eating in Simon's house.
So she came carrying an alabaster flask of perfume.
Think about that for a moment.
She knew where she was going.
She knew whose house it was.
She knew the kind of people who might be there.
And she went anyway.
Some of us understand that kind of courage.
The courage it takes to walk back into church after people have heard about your failure.
The courage it takes to pray after falling into the same sin you promised God you would never commit again.
The courage it takes to admit that the marriage is struggling, the addiction has returned, the anger is consuming you, or the secret you have hidden for years is slowly destroying your peace.
Sometimes the hardest journey toward Jesus is not measured in miles.
It is measured in how much shame you must walk through to reach Him.
The woman entered the house.
And then something happened that nobody at that table could ignore.
She stood behind Jesus at His feet, weeping.
Her tears began to wet His feet.
She wiped them with her hair.
She kissed His feet.
And she anointed them with perfume.
Luke describes the scene without giving us a transcript of her thoughts.
We are not told exactly why she cried.
But we are shown that her tears were real, her humility was visible, and her love was costly.
She did not deliver a speech defending her reputation.
She did not demand that Simon understand her.
She simply came to Jesus.
And in a room where one man was quietly judging her, Jesus allowed her to remain at His feet.
That detail matters.
Because Simon was watching.
And what he saw did not impress him.
It offended him.
Luke 7:39 records Simon's private judgment. He reasoned that if Jesus were truly a prophet, He would know what kind of woman was touching Him.
Simon thought he had discovered something disqualifying about Jesus.
But the very thing he believed Jesus failed to know was the thing Jesus understood perfectly.
Jesus knew the woman was a sinner.
He also knew what Simon was thinking.
And that is when Jesus told a story.
Not a long story.
Not a complicated theological lecture.
Just two people.
Two debts.
And one creditor.
Jesus said, in Luke 7:41–42:
“A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they couldn't pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?”
A denarius was commonly associated with a day's wage for a laborer.
One debtor owed five hundred denarii.
The other owed fifty.
One debt was ten times larger than the other.
But Jesus placed both debtors in exactly the same impossible position.
Neither could pay.
Read that again.
The difference between their debts was enormous.
The difference between their ability to save themselves was nonexistent.
Neither could pay.
And this is where the story stops being about two imaginary borrowers and begins confronting every human heart.
Some people have sins that became public scandals.
Others have sins that remain hidden beneath a respectable appearance.
Some have destroyed relationships through betrayal.
Others have spent years quietly nurturing bitterness, pride, envy, or contempt.
Some have rebelled against God openly.
Others have learned to disguise their rebellion beneath religious language.
The consequences and seriousness of particular sins are not always identical.
But before a holy God, none of us can purchase our own forgiveness.
Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
The Greek word used there is ἥμαρτον (hēmarton), from the verb hamartanō, meaning “to sin.”
And Romans 3:24 immediately points to the hope sinners desperately need: justification by God's grace as a gift, through the redemption found in Christ Jesus.
That is the Gospel.
Not that your debt was small enough to overlook.
Not that your good deeds finally outweighed your failures.
Not that your religious activities made you worthy of acceptance.
But that salvation comes through the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
And in the parable, Jesus says something breathtaking.
The creditor forgave them both.
The Greek text uses the word:
ἐχαρίσατο — echarisato
It comes from charizomai, a verb associated with graciously giving, granting, or forgiving.
In the context of the parable, the creditor freely canceled what the debtors could not repay.
They did not negotiate smaller payments.
They did not promise to work harder.
They did not earn the cancellation.
The creditor forgave them.
And Jesus asked Simon:
“Which of them therefore will love him most?”
Simon answered:
“I suppose he to whom he forgave the most.”
Jesus replied:
“You have judged correctly.” — Luke 7:43
But Jesus was not finished.
Because the story was not merely about money.
It was about the woman standing at His feet.
And the man sitting at His table.
Then came one of the most piercing moments in the entire account.
Jesus turned toward the woman and spoke to Simon.
“Do you see this woman?” — Luke 7:44
What a question.
Of course Simon could see her.
He had been watching her.
He had already judged her.
He had already formed his conclusion about what her presence meant.
But Jesus asked whether he truly saw her.
There is a difference between looking at someone and seeing them.
Simon saw a reputation.
Jesus saw a person.
Simon saw a reason for rejection.
Jesus recognized the significance of her love.
Simon was occupied with what she had been.
Jesus was about to declare what God's forgiveness meant for her.
And suddenly the entire room became a mirror.
Because we do this too.
We see someone's divorce before we see their grief.
We see someone's addiction before we see their struggle.
We see someone's prison record before we see their repentance.
We see someone's scandal before we consider what Christ might be doing in their heart.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we become so confident in our ability to identify another person's sin that we forget how desperately we ourselves need mercy.
Jesus then compared Simon's welcome with the woman's actions.
Simon had provided no water for Jesus' feet.
The woman had wet His feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
Simon had offered no kiss of greeting.
The woman had not stopped kissing Jesus' feet.
Simon had not anointed His head with oil.
The woman had anointed His feet with perfume.
These were acts of hospitality and honor, expressed in different ways.
The text does not require us to conclude that Simon had violated a universal religious law by omitting them.
But Jesus used the contrast to expose something far more important than etiquette.
The woman had demonstrated extraordinary love.
Simon had shown comparatively little.
And then Jesus said the words that explain the entire encounter.
“Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But to whom little is forgiven, the same loves little.” — Luke 7:47
This verse must be understood carefully.
Jesus was not teaching that the woman purchased forgiveness with tears, perfume, or affection.
That would contradict the very parable He had just told.
In the parable, forgiveness comes first.
Love follows.
The debt is canceled.
Then the forgiven debtor responds with love.
The Greek expression in Luke 7:47 includes:
ἀφέωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι αὐτῆς αἱ πολλαί
apheōntai hai hamartiai autēs hai pollai
“Her many sins have been forgiven.”
The verb apheōntai expresses a completed forgiveness with continuing significance.
The following phrase, ὅτι ἠγάπησεν πολύ (hoti ēgapēsen poly), is often translated “for she loved much.”
In context, her great love is best understood as evidence of forgiveness, not the price paid to obtain it.
Jesus Himself confirms the foundation of her salvation in verse 50:
“Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”
Not “Your perfume has saved you.”
Not “Your tears have purchased your forgiveness.”
Not “Your public display has earned you a place in God's kingdom.”
Your faith has saved you.
Her love was the beautiful response of a heart receiving mercy.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because if forgiveness could be purchased through enough tears, some of us would spend our entire lives wondering whether we had cried enough.
If forgiveness could be earned through enough religious activity, we would never know whether we had finally done enough.
If forgiveness depended on the approval of respectable people, many wounded sinners would never dare approach Jesus.
But the Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He did not come to make sin harmless.
He did not come to declare evil good.
He came to deal with sin through His own saving work.
At the cross, Jesus bore the judgment sinners deserve.
Through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed to those who repent and believe.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works.
And the grace that saves us does not leave us comfortable in the sins that once enslaved us.
It calls us into repentance.
It teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
It begins transforming the way we think, love, forgive, and live.
This is why the woman in Simon's house is not merely a moving example of emotional worship.
She confronts us with the transforming power of divine mercy.
Her story does not glorify her sin.
It glorifies the Savior who forgives sinners.
And here is the part that may be hardest to accept.
Simon was physically closer to the table of religious respectability.
But the woman demonstrated a deeper appreciation for forgiveness.
He had invited Jesus into his house.
She responded to Jesus with remarkable love.
He was evaluating Jesus.
She was honoring Him.
He questioned whether Jesus knew her sins.
Jesus showed that He knew both her condition and Simon's heart.
That should make every Christian examine something.
Have we become so familiar with the language of grace that we no longer marvel at it?
Have we become so practiced at identifying other people's failures that we have forgotten to confess our own?
Have we learned to sing about forgiveness while quietly refusing to forgive?
Have we mistaken being religiously informed for being spiritually transformed?
You can know Bible verses and still be proud.
You can attend worship services and still be cruel.
You can serve in ministry and still hide bitterness.
You can speak passionately about holiness while treating broken people as though they are beyond the reach of God's mercy.
And none of us should assume that we are immune to these dangers.
Because Simon's greatest problem was not that he had too much knowledge.
It was that his judgment of the woman revealed how little he appreciated the mercy she had received.
The question Jesus asked still echoes.
“Do you see this woman?”
Do you see the person you have reduced to their worst mistake?
Do you see the believer who has fallen and is struggling to stand again?
Do you see the family member whose past has become the only story you are willing to remember?
And perhaps most painfully...
Can you see yourself without pretending that you have never needed forgiveness?
There is no spiritual maturity in minimizing sin.
But there is no Christlike maturity in pretending that grace belongs only to people whose sins are socially acceptable.
The ground at the foot of the cross leaves no room for boasting.
The proud need repentance.
The ashamed need the Gospel.
The outwardly respectable need mercy.
The publicly disgraced need mercy.
We all need Jesus.
And perhaps tonight someone reading this is carrying a burden that nobody else knows about.
You have smiled through conversations while quietly wondering whether God is tired of you.
You have listened to sermons about forgiveness while remembering things you wish you could erase.
You have asked yourself whether your failures have disqualified you from ever becoming the person you once hoped to be.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is not something to excuse.
But neither is it something you must hide from the Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
You do not need to invent a cleaner history before coming to Christ.
You need to come honestly.
Confess what is wrong.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Trust the crucified and risen Jesus.
Receive the grace that cannot be earned.
And begin walking in the new life He calls you to live.
First John 1:9 gives believers this assurance: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
A damaged relationship may require years of rebuilding.
A broken trust may require patient accountability.
A sinful pattern may require serious repentance, practical changes, wise pastoral care, and ongoing support.
Grace does not erase the importance of truth, justice, or responsibility.
But grace means that your past does not have the final authority to define your standing before God when you belong to Jesus Christ.
The cross speaks a greater word.
And in Luke 7, Jesus speaks directly to the woman.
“Your sins are forgiven.” — Luke 7:48
Imagine hearing those words.
Not from the people who had judged her.
Not from someone who barely knew her.
But from Jesus.
The other guests began asking among themselves who this was who even forgave sins.
They were encountering a question at the very heart of Jesus' identity and authority.
And then Jesus said to the woman:
“Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.” — Luke 7:50
The Greek word translated “peace” is εἰρήνη (eirēnē).
It carries the sense of peace and well-being, resonating with the rich biblical understanding of peace associated with the Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (shalom).
Jesus was not merely telling her to stop crying.
He was sending her away with the assurance of salvation and peace.
Luke does not tell us everything that happened afterward.
We are not given a detailed account of how the townspeople treated her the next morning.
We are not told whether every damaged relationship was restored.
We are not told that her life suddenly became easy.
And we should not pretend Scripture tells us what it does not.
But we know what Jesus declared.
Her sins were forgiven.
Her faith had saved her.
She could go in peace.
The people in that room might have remembered her reputation.
But Jesus had pronounced forgiveness.
And sometimes that is where a new life begins.
Not when everyone finally understands your story.
Not when every critic apologizes.
Not when the consequences of your past have vanished.
But when you stop building your identity around what sin has done and begin living by faith in what Christ has accomplished.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus is mighty to save.
Because the cross is sufficient.
Because the resurrection is real.
Because the mercy of God reaches sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And because Jesus does not merely improve the ending of a broken story.
He redeems people and transforms their lives.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending to be perfect.
Not to turn brokenness into entertainment.
Not to make merchandise, personalities, or popularity the center of the message.
But to keep pointing wounded, searching, struggling, growing people back to Jesus Christ and the truth of His Word.
If this message has uncovered something in your heart, don't rush past that moment.
Maybe you have been hiding behind religious activity.
Maybe you have been carrying shame that Christ calls you to bring into the light.
Maybe you have been judging someone whom God is calling you to love with truth and compassion.
Maybe you have forgotten what it felt like to be overwhelmed by the wonder of forgiveness.
You can respond right where you are.
Pray honestly.

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. Forgive me. Expose the pride I have refused to see and the wounds I have tried to hide. Teach me to repent sincerely, to trust Your grace, and to love others as someone who has received mercy. Change my heart. Make my life a testimony to Your truth, not my own goodness. Amen.”
And if you are willing, make the comments a place of honest faith rather than religious performance.
You do not have to expose private details or publicly confess sensitive sins to prove your sincerity. God hears the prayers nobody else can see.
But your testimony, even in a few words, may encourage someone who has been afraid to come back to Christ.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to suggest you know everything about their life.
But because the message of Jesus' forgiveness deserves to reach people who have nearly given up hope.
We want this to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, repentance is preached faithfully, forgiveness is celebrated gratefully, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
And if you believe this mission is worth sustaining, I want to invite you into something deeper.

It is a voluntary act of support for this particular Gospel ministry—an opportunity to give generously toward the continued creation, development, and expansion of Christ-centered teaching, devotional content, and discipleship resources.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure or compulsion. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of fear.
But because supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way of glorifying Him with the resources He has entrusted to you.

And if this ministry has encouraged your faith, helped you return to Scripture, or reminded you that Jesus has not abandoned His people, perhaps you would prayerfully consider helping us reach the next person who desperately needs to hear that same truth.
Sharing can help a message travel.
But only Jesus Christ can save a soul.
That distinction will never change.
Before you leave, return one last time to the house of Simon.
Picture the table.
The guests.
The religious man who thought he understood the situation.
The woman whose past was known.
The tears falling onto Jesus' feet.
The perfume.
The uncomfortable silence.
And the Savior who knew everything.
Jesus did not need Simon to explain the woman's reputation.
He did not need the woman to prove that her sins were insignificant.
He knew the truth.
And He spoke forgiveness.
Perhaps that is the most astonishing part of the entire story.
The woman did not encounter a Savior who was ignorant of her sin.
She encountered a Savior whose mercy was greater than the debt she could never repay.
And that is the hope of every repentant sinner who comes to Christ.
Not that Jesus knows less about us than other people do.
But that He knows us completely, and His saving grace is sufficient.
So when shame tells you to run away, remember the woman who came to His feet.
When pride tells you that you are better than the person beside you, remember Simon.
When guilt tells you that you must somehow repay God before He will receive you, remember the two debtors.
And when the enemy tries to convince you that your worst chapter must become your final chapter, remember the cross and the empty tomb.
Because the last word over a life surrendered to Jesus does not belong to the scandal.
It belongs to the Savior.
The most beautiful thing about that woman's story is not that Jesus overlooked her past—but that He knew her sins, forgave her, and sent her away in peace.
